prompt: R1 uses local enable authentication. Both an enable secret and a different enable password exist at privilege 15. Which credential moves you from `>` to `#`?
options: The password configured as the enable password
Either configured credential, tried in sequence
The password configured as the enable secret
The shared password under the console line
explanation: For the same privilege level, the enable secret takes precedence over the enable password.

whyWrong.0: The enable password is ignored when an enable secret exists.
whyWrong.1: There is no fallback to the enable password.
whyWrong.3: Console line authentication is separate from the enable transition.

prompt: On traditional IOS, what does `service password-encryption` do to applicable cleartext password fields?
options: Stores those fields using reversible type 7 obfuscation
Replaces those fields with type 9 password verifiers
Encrypts terminal traffic for existing Telnet sessions
Converts the enable secret into a stronger hash
explanation: `service password-encryption` obscures cleartext password fields with reversible type 7. It does not encrypt sessions or upgrade the enable secret.

whyWrong.1: It does not select type 9 (scrypt) for those fields.
whyWrong.2: It protects stored text, not a Telnet session.
whyWrong.3: It does not change the hash on the enable secret.

prompt: An IOS configuration contains `enable secret 5` followed by a stored verifier. What does the number identify?
options: The privilege level assigned to the enable session
The type of password verifier stored in the configuration
The number of failed logins permitted before disconnection
The minimum number of characters in the original password
explanation: The number in `enable secret 5` is the verifier type; type 5 is the legacy MD5-based hash. A hash can still be guessed, so it is not uncrackable.

whyWrong.0: The type does not set a privilege level.
whyWrong.2: Login retry limits are separate configuration.
whyWrong.3: The type does not encode password length.

prompt: A powered router has no usable IP interface. Which access method still works for an authorized technician with the correct cable?
options: An SSH session to its previous interface address
An HTTPS session to its previous interface address
A Telnet session to its default gateway address
A direct connection to its serial console
explanation: A serial console connection needs no IP interface. It still requires valid credentials if the console is configured to ask for them.

whyWrong.0: SSH needs a reachable IP address on the router.
whyWrong.1: HTTPS management also needs IP reachability.
whyWrong.2: A gateway address is not a management address on the router.

prompt: Which two identity settings are used by the conventional unnamed RSA-key workflow taught in this chapter? Choose two.
options: An available public DNS resolver
A configured nondefault hostname
An established Telnet session from the client
A configured management-interface IP address
A configured local domain name
explanation: The conventional workflow generates the RSA key from a configured hostname and domain name. This is the chapter’s workflow, not every possible key method.

whyWrong.0: The key identity does not need a DNS lookup.
whyWrong.2: A Telnet session is not needed to generate the key.
whyWrong.3: An IP address gives reachability but is not part of the key identity.

prompt: Which command saves the verified running configuration for the normal next boot?
options: `copy running-config startup-config`
`copy startup-config running-config`
`show startup-config`
`configure terminal`
explanation: The source comes first and the destination second, so `copy running-config startup-config` saves the active configuration for the next boot.

whyWrong.1: This copies saved settings into the active configuration.
whyWrong.2: This displays the saved configuration without changing it.
whyWrong.3: This enters configuration mode and saves nothing.

prompt: With ordinary IOS privilege levels, which two actions require privileged EXEC? Choose two.
options: Send a basic ping permitted in user EXEC
Read the device hostname from its prompt
Inspect the full running configuration
Enter a username at a login prompt
Enter global configuration mode
explanation: Showing the full running configuration and entering global configuration mode need privileged EXEC.

whyWrong.0: A basic ping works in user EXEC.
whyWrong.1: The hostname shows in any prompt.
whyWrong.3: Entering a username is part of login, not privileged EXEC.

prompt: With local authentication and no custom authorization, which account and line combination begins a session at privilege 15?
options: A default-privilege local user on a line using `login local`
A shared line password with `login` and an enable secret
A local user with `secret` but no configured privilege
A privilege-15 local user on a line using `login local`
explanation: A local user starts at privilege 1 unless configured otherwise. A privilege-15 user on a line with `login local` starts at privileged EXEC.

whyWrong.1: A shared line password with an enable secret starts at privilege 1.

prompt: A client gets no ping replies from R1, but a new SSH login to R1 succeeds. What does this show?
options: SSH access works even though this ICMP test did not receive replies
The successful SSH login proves ICMP is enabled on every interface
The failed ping proves the SSH session is connected to another subnet
The client must regenerate R1’s SSH host keys before continuing
explanation: SSH and ICMP are separate protocols, so SSH can work while ping gets no replies. Record each result separately.

whyWrong.1: A working SSH login says nothing about ICMP on other interfaces.
whyWrong.2: A failed ping does not identify the SSH session’s subnet.
whyWrong.3: A successful login gives no reason to regenerate host keys.

exhibit.title: R1# show ip ssh — legacy image
exhibit.text:
SSH Enabled - version 1.99
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3

prompt: A legacy IOS image reports the SSH version shown. Which configuration restricts that server to SSHv2?
options: `transport input telnet` under the VTY lines
`service password-encryption` in global configuration mode
`ip ssh version 2` in global configuration mode
`login local` under the console and VTY lines
explanation: Version 1.99 means the server accepts SSHv1 and SSHv2. `ip ssh version 2` restricts it to SSHv2.

whyWrong.0: `transport input telnet` permits Telnet and does not set the SSH version.

prompt: Which two statements correctly distinguish management access methods? Choose two.
options: A direct serial console can work without a configured IP interface
SSH always proves that a physically separate management network is used
An HTTP management page protects credentials in the same way as HTTPS
TACACS+ and RADIUS support AAA decisions rather than replacing SSH
Cloud management requires every product to disable local access
explanation: A serial console works without an IP interface. TACACS+ and RADIUS provide AAA decisions while the administrator still connects with SSH.

whyWrong.1: Whether management is in-band or out-of-band is a design choice, not a property of SSH.
whyWrong.2: HTTPS adds TLS; plain HTTP does not protect credentials.
whyWrong.4: Cloud management does not require disabling local access.

exhibit.title: Terminal sessions — representative excerpt
exhibit.text:
Line       User       Host(s)   Idle       Location
*  0 con 0                idle      00:00:00
   2 vty 0     admin      idle      00:00:05   10.8.0.10

prompt: Which command most directly provides the terminal-session table shown, including the Location column?
options: `show ip ssh`
`show privilege`
`show users`
`show ip interface brief`
explanation: `show users` lists active lines and users, with the client address under Location for remote sessions. The asterisk marks your own session.

whyWrong.0: `show ip ssh` shows SSH server settings.
whyWrong.1: `show privilege` shows your current privilege level.
whyWrong.3: `show ip interface brief` shows interface addresses and state.

prompt: The intended idle timeout is five minutes on VTY 0–4. You are at the prompt shown. Which next command selects the correct configuration context?
options: line vty 0 4
exec-timeout 5 0
interface gigabitethernet0/0
enable
explanation: At the global configuration prompt, enter `line vty 0 4` first. Then `exec-timeout 5 0` applies under the config-line prompt.

whyWrong.1: `exec-timeout` belongs under line configuration, not at the global prompt.
whyWrong.2: An interface is not the context for an idle timeout.
whyWrong.3: `enable` enters privileged EXEC; you are already configuring.

prompt: A previously trusted SSH server presents a different host key. A planned router replacement might explain it, but you have not verified the replacement record. What should you do before accepting the new key?
options: Accept the key because a successful IP test proves the server identity.
Verify the expected device and new key through the trusted management process.
Delete the old key record and retry with the same username and password.
Change the VTY transport to Telnet until the client stops reporting the warning.
explanation: A host-key change can be legitimate, but the warning does not prove it. Confirm the device and its new key through the trusted management process before accepting.

whyWrong.0: IP reachability does not authenticate the server.
whyWrong.2: Deleting the stored key removes the check without answering the identity question.
whyWrong.3: Falling back to Telnet verifies nothing and removes encryption.

exhibit.title: Representative access checks
exhibit.text:
New SSH login: refused before authentication
Ping to management address: replies
SSH server: enabled, version 2.0
Local user: confirmed present
Only VTY range:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input telnet

prompt: Which narrow change meets the requirement to admit SSH and reject Telnet?
options: Replace local-user authentication with a shared VTY line password.
Replace transport input telnet with transport input ssh on the VTY range.
Create another administrator at privilege 15 in the local username database.
Save the current configuration, then repeat the same new-session test.
explanation: The VTY range accepts Telnet only. `transport input ssh` makes it accept SSH only; then test a new session.

whyWrong.0: Authentication method does not change which transport the range accepts.
whyWrong.2: Another user does not change the accepted transport.

exhibit.title: Abbreviated VTY configuration
exhibit.text:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
line vty 5 15
 password 7 0822455D0A16
 login
 transport input telnet

prompt: A device has VTY 0–15. Which problem is demonstrated by this abbreviated configuration?
options: Each VTY range needs its own independently generated SSH host key.
The ranges use different authentication methods and accept different transports.
The local username database applies only to the lowest numbered VTY range.
The higher VTY range inherits SSH-only policy when the first range is occupied.
explanation: VTY 5–15 still allows Telnet with shared-line authentication, while 0–4 uses local users and SSH. Each range has its own policy, so apply it to every range.

whyWrong.0: One host key serves all VTY lines.
whyWrong.2: The local database is not limited to certain lines; each line picks its authentication.
whyWrong.3: A range does not inherit another range’s transport policy.

exhibit.title: Representative console review and client evidence
exhibit.text:
ADMIN can reach R1 at its configured 10.8.0.1 address.
Hostname: R1
Local domain: not configured
RSA host-key inventory: no generated key pair
Local user admin: present, privilege 15
All VTY lines: login local; transport input ssh
SSH server: disabled

prompt: R1 uses the conventional hostname/domain/RSA-key workflow. Which ordered correction addresses the missing SSH prerequisites without changing the working IP path or local login policy?
options: Set a reachable DNS server and default route, then retry the existing SSH server.
Create another privilege-15 user and save; the VTY settings generate the host key.
Replace login local with a line password, then permit SSH and Telnet together.
Set the local domain, generate the supported RSA host key, and require SSHv2.
explanation: The IP path and local user do not provide a host key. Set the domain name, generate the RSA key, and require SSHv2, then verify a fresh login. DNS is not needed for the domain name.

whyWrong.0: A DNS server and route do not create a host key.
whyWrong.1: A new user and a save do not generate a key.
whyWrong.2: A shared line password and Telnet do not give SSH-only access.

exhibit.title: Representative console review and new-session test
exhibit.text:
Fresh SSH test: server reached; username/password authentication fails.
All VTY lines:
 login local
 transport input ssh
Complete username check: no username entries
AAA method lists: none configured
An enable secret exists; the console session remains open.

prompt: Which correction addresses the failed login while preserving named-user authentication?
options: Add a shared line password while leaving the empty local database selected.
Change the interface subnet before another username/password attempt.
Use the enable secret as an implicit replacement for the missing username.
Create the intended local username and secret through the working console.
explanation: The VTY lines use local-user authentication, but the local database has no accounts. Create the account at the console, then test a new session.

whyWrong.0: A shared line password is not used with `login local`.
whyWrong.1: The session already reaches authentication, so addressing is not the problem.
whyWrong.2: The enable secret does not stand in for a login username.

exhibit.title: Representative complete relevant VTY excerpts
exhibit.text:
RUNNING-CONFIG
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh

STARTUP-CONFIG
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input telnet

Normal boot is configured to load startup-config.

prompt: The policy requires SSH-only access after a normal reboot. Current new SSH succeeds and new Telnet is refused. What must be corrected before declaring the saved policy complete?
options: Generate another RSA key because running and startup transports differ.
Remove the local user because it appears in both configuration stores.
Save the verified running configuration and inspect the saved VTY policy.
Merge the startup configuration into running to make both stores agree.
explanation: The verified SSH-only policy exists only in running-config. Save running to startup and check the saved VTY lines.

whyWrong.0: Differing transports are a persistence problem, not a key problem.
whyWrong.1: The local account belongs in both configurations.
whyWrong.3: Merging startup into running can restore the old Telnet policy.

exhibit.title: Representative policy review
exhibit.text:
REQUIREMENT
admin: initial privilege 15
auditor: initial privilege 1
Remote terminals: SSH only; local-user authentication
Only VTY lines 0–4 exist. No custom AAA authorization.

RUNNING-CONFIG
username admin privilege 15 secret <stored verifier>
username auditor privilege 15 secret <stored verifier>
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input telnet ssh

prompt: Review the requirement and active configuration. Which pair of corrections meets the access policy while retaining the working admin account?
options: Set both local users to privilege 1 and leave both VTY transports enabled.
Delete auditor and replace login local with a shared line password.
Change the console timeout and save without changing the username or transports.
Set auditor to privilege 1 and restrict the VTY range to SSH.
explanation: The policy sets initial privilege per local user and restricts the incoming transport. Set auditor to privilege 1 and limit the VTY range to SSH; keep admin as is.

whyWrong.0: Admin must start at privilege 15, and Telnet must go.
whyWrong.1: Deleting a required account and using a shared password breaks the policy.
whyWrong.2: A console timeout fixes neither mismatch.

prompt: Which TCP ports do SSH and Telnet use?
options: SSH 22, Telnet 23
SSH 23, Telnet 22
SSH 22, Telnet 25
SSH 443, Telnet 23
explanation: SSH uses TCP 22 and Telnet uses TCP 23.

prompt: Which command reports the SSH server configuration, such as the enabled version?
options: show ip ssh
show ssh
show users
show privilege
explanation: `show ip ssh` reports the SSH server configuration. `show ssh` reports SSH sessions.

whyWrong.1: `show ssh` lists SSH sessions, not server settings.
whyWrong.2: `show users` lists active terminal lines and users.
whyWrong.3: `show privilege` shows your current privilege level.

prompt: What are the default console line settings on classic IOS?
options: 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit
115200 baud, 7 data bits, even parity, 1 stop bit
9600 baud, 8 data bits, odd parity, 2 stop bits
19200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit
explanation: The console defaults to 9600 baud, 8-N-1, with no console password.

whyWrong.1: 115200 baud and even parity are not the defaults.
whyWrong.2: The default is no parity and 1 stop bit.

prompt: What is the default `exec-timeout` on an IOS line?
options: 10 minutes
5 minutes
30 minutes
No timeout
explanation: The default `exec-timeout` is 10 minutes of idle time.

whyWrong.1: 5 minutes is the value the lab sets, not the default.
whyWrong.2: 30 minutes is not the IOS default.
whyWrong.3: A default idle timeout exists, so it is not disabled.
